triage.name: Athlete's Foot
triage.reason: Common pruritic scaly rash of the feet with a clear diagnosis by history and exam, plus KOH testing; good for teaching dermatologic description and risk factors.

demographics: More common in adolescents and adult men
Common in people who use communal showers, pools, or gyms
More frequent in warm, humid climates and in the summer months

risk_factors.text: Walking barefoot in locker rooms, public showers, or pool decks
Excessive sweating of the feet or wearing occlusive shoes all day
Sharing shoes, socks, or towels with an affected person
Peripheral vascular disease or venous stasis

family_history: Often a household member with the same foot rash or fungal nail infection
social_history: Occupational exposure to wet floors (e.g., pool staff, cleaners)
exposures: Communal showers or locker room floors

chief_complaints.text: The skin between my toes is itchy and peeling
My feet itch and burn, especially at night
The skin on my feet is cracked and scaly
My feet smell bad and the skin looks white and soggy

hpi.onset: Gradual over days to weeks; often noticed after a gym, pool, or shower exposure
hpi.duration: Usually present for 1–4 weeks before the patient seeks care; may be recurrent over months or years
hpi.progression: Starts between the toes, especially the fourth and fifth web space, then spreads to the sole or dorsum; may wax and wane
hpi.location: Most often the web spaces between the toes, especially between the fourth and fifth toes; can involve the sole, heel, or top of the foot
hpi.quality: Itchy, burning, peeling, cracked, or macerated skin
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; itching can be intense and disrupt sleep
hpi.timing: Itching is often worse at night or after removing shoes and socks
aggravating: Walking barefoot in public showers or locker rooms

associated_symptoms.text: Peeling or scaling between the toes
Burning or stinging of the feet
White, soggy, macerated skin between the toes
Small blisters or vesicles on the sole or instep
Painful cracking or fissures of the heel or sole
Red, scaly rash in the groin or on the hands

pertinent_negatives: Redness spreading rapidly up the leg
Severe pain out of proportion to the rash
Numbness or loss of sensation in the feet
Known psoriasis or eczema of the feet

positives.text: Itchy, scaly rash between the toes
Peeling or flaking skin on the soles

negatives: Rash on the palms or trunk
argues_against: Rash involving the palms and soles with nail pitting (psoriasis)
Sharply demarcated plaques with silvery scale
Acute monoarthritis of the great toe (gout)

negatives: Numbness or tingling in the feet
argues_against: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy as the primary cause of foot symptoms

negatives: New soap, detergent, or shoe material exposure
argues_against: Contact dermatitis from footwear or topical products

atypical.how_it_differs: Often presents with itching and peeling between the toes, but young children may not localize symptoms and instead show fussiness or scratching at the feet; the rash may be mistaken for eczema or diaper rash if it involves the soles.
missing_classic_features: Clear description of itching between the toes

atypical.how_it_differs: May have less itching and more dry, cracked, scaly skin on the soles, which can be mistaken for dry skin or eczema; diabetes and poor circulation increase the risk of more extensive or stubborn infection.
Athlete's foot can be more extensive, slower to heal, and more likely to lead to bacterial cellulitis or foot ulcers; sensory neuropathy may blunt the itching and pain.
The infection may be more widespread, involve the soles and dorsum extensively, and respond more slowly to topical therapy; risk of secondary bacterial infection is higher.
missing_classic_features: Localized rash limited to the toe web spaces

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; normal gait
general.moderate: Well-appearing; may scratch at the feet or shift weight off the affected foot
general.severe: Well-appearing but uncomfortable; limping or avoiding weight on a fissured foot
general.critical: Ill-appearing with systemic signs (fever, spreading erythema, purulence) suggesting secondary bacterial infection rather than uncomplicated tinea pedis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the web spaces between all toes, spreading the toes apart
findings.finding: White, soggy, macerated skin with peeling and fissuring, most often between the fourth and fifth toes

findings.maneuver: Inspect the interdigital skin after drying
findings.finding: Erythema with fine scaling and a slightly raised, advancing edge
Diffuse dry scaling, sometimes in a moccasin-like distribution over the sole and heel

findings.maneuver: Inspect the heel and interdigital spaces
findings.finding: Painful cracks or fissures of the skin

findings.maneuver: Note any odor when removing socks or examining the feet

findings.finding: Thickened, yellow-brown, crumbling, or distally separated nails

findings.maneuver: Inspect the dorsum of the foot
findings.finding: Scaling or erythema extending onto the top of the foot

findings.maneuver: Inspect the rash for pustules or honey-colored crust
Palpate the leg and foot for warmth, tenderness, and spreading erythema
findings.finding: No warmth, tenderness, or erythema extending up the leg

findings.maneuver: Inspect the sole and between the toes for breaks in the skin
findings.finding: No ulcer or full-thickness skin defect

findings.maneuver: Test sensation with monofilament or light touch, especially if diabetes is present
Inspect and palpate the joints of the foot and ankle
findings.finding: No joint swelling, warmth, or redness
No sterile pustules or sharply demarcated silvery plaques on the palms and soles

initial.why: First-line bedside test: scraped scale from the active edge or macerated web space shows branching septate hyphae, confirming a dermatophyte infection
Identifies the species when the diagnosis is uncertain or the rash fails topical therapy
initial.only_if: KOH is negative but tinea pedis is still suspected, or the infection is not responding to treatment

supporting.why: Helps distinguish dermatophyte infection from erythrasma or other causes of interdigital scaling
supporting.only_if: the diagnosis is unclear after KOH testing

not_indicated.why: No role in a localized superficial fungal infection; a normal white count is expected
Inflammatory markers are not useful for tinea pedis
Not helpful in superficial fungal skin infection
Not needed to diagnose athlete's foot; check only if diabetes is suspected or already known
Not part of the workup for athlete's foot
Only if secondary bacterial infection is suspected; not routine for uncomplicated tinea pedis
No bony abnormality in athlete's foot; imaging does not help
Not indicated for a superficial skin infection

decision_points: Confirm the diagnosis with KOH microscopy before starting systemic therapy or when the rash does not respond to topical antifungals
Look for onychomycosis and treat it, since infected nails are a reservoir for recurrent tinea pedis
In diabetes or immunosuppression, examine carefully for fissures, ulcers, and secondary bacterial infection

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Both cause a red, warm, painful foot; cellulitis can complicate or mimic tinea pedis.
differential.trigger: Rapidly spreading redness, fever, or systemic symptoms

history: Acute onset over hours to days
Pain out of proportion to skin findings
exam: Diffuse erythema, warmth, and tenderness without scaling or maceration
imaging: Not routinely needed; consider ultrasound if abscess suspected

differential.name: Contact dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Itchy, red, scaly rash on the feet, often triggered by shoes or topical products.

history: Exposure to new shoes, socks, or topical agents
Itching and burning without a musty odor
exam: Erythema and scaling on the dorsum or areas of contact, often sparing the web spaces
Sharp demarcation at the shoe line

differential.name: Psoriasis
differential.why_considered: Scaly plaques on the soles and between toes can resemble tinea pedis.

history: Personal or family history of psoriasis
exam: Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale, often on soles and palms
No central clearing or advancing border

differential.name: Erythrasma
differential.why_considered: Interdigital scaling and maceration caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum.

history: May have similar rash in groin or axillae

differential.name: Pitted keratolysis
differential.why_considered: Causes small pits and maceration on the soles, often with odor.

exam: Multiple small punched-out pits on the soles, especially weight-bearing areas

differential.name: Dyshidrotic eczema
differential.why_considered: Vesicular rash on the soles and palms that can be itchy.

history: Often associated with atopy or stress
exam: Deep-seated vesicles on the instep and palms
Scaling and fissures after vesicles resolve

severity.mild: Mild itching and scaling limited to the toe web spaces; no fissures or secondary infection.
severity.moderate: More extensive scaling, maceration, and fissures involving the sole or multiple web spaces; itching interferes with sleep.
severity.severe: Extensive involvement of the sole and dorsum, painful fissures, and possible secondary bacterial infection; may require systemic antifungal therapy.

red_flags.finding: Rapidly spreading redness, warmth, and swelling of the foot or leg
red_flags.meaning: Suggests bacterial cellulitis, which requires prompt antibiotic treatment.
Indicates possible systemic infection or severe secondary bacterial infection.
Suggests secondary bacterial infection or abscess.

red_flags.finding: Severe pain out of proportion to skin findings
red_flags.meaning: May indicate deeper infection such as abscess or necrotizing fasciitis.
Suggests necrotizing infection or severe vascular compromise; emergency.

red_flags.finding: Numbness or loss of sensation in the feet
red_flags.meaning: May indicate peripheral neuropathy, increasing risk of unnoticed injury and infection.

complications.name: Recurrence
clues: Untreated onychomycosis or continued exposure to damp environments

special_populations.differences: May present with itching and peeling between toes, but young children may not localize symptoms; rash may be mistaken for eczema.
Less itching and more dry, cracked, scaly skin on the soles; may be mistaken for dry skin or eczema; diabetes and poor circulation increase risk of complications.
More extensive, slower to heal, and higher risk of bacterial cellulitis or foot ulcers; sensory neuropathy may blunt itching and pain.
Infection may be more widespread, involve soles and dorsum extensively, respond more slowly to topical therapy, and have higher risk of secondary bacterial infection.

key_questions.question: Where exactly on your feet did the rash start, and where is it now?
key_questions.looking_for: Starts between the toes, especially the fourth and fifth web space, then may spread to the sole or top of the foot

key_questions.question: How long has it been there, and is it getting better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days to weeks; may wax and wane or recur over months

key_questions.question: What does the skin look like and feel like?
key_questions.looking_for: Itchy, peeling, cracked, scaly, or white and soggy skin between the toes

key_questions.question: Does it itch or burn, and when is it worst?
key_questions.looking_for: Itching or burning, often worse at night or after removing shoes and socks

key_questions.question: What makes it better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with sweating, closed shoes, warm humid weather; better with dry feet, sandals, or antifungal cream

key_questions.question: Do you walk barefoot in locker rooms, public showers, or around pools?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposure to damp communal floors, a classic risk factor

key_questions.question: Do your feet sweat a lot, or do you wear closed shoes all day?
Does anyone at home have the same foot rash or thick, discolored toenails?
key_questions.looking_for: Household member with tinea pedis or onychomycosis; shared footwear or towels

key_questions.question: Have you had this before, and did anything treat it?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior episodes or partial response to over-the-counter antifungals

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, poor circulation, or a weakened immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, venous insufficiency, or immunosuppression; raises risk of complications

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medicines that suppress the immune system, like prednisone or a biologic?
key_questions.looking_for: Corticosteroids, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, methotrexate, or TNF inhibitors

key_questions.question: Have you used any creams, powders, or home remedies on it?
key_questions.looking_for: Antifungal use, steroid creams, or other topical products that may change the appearance

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, chills, or redness spreading up your leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in uncomplicated tinea pedis; present suggests cellulitis or systemic infection

key_questions.question: Is the pain severe, or is there pus or a foul-smelling discharge?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests secondary bacterial infection or deeper infection

key_questions.question: Any numbness, tingling, or loss of feeling in your feet?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests peripheral neuropathy and higher risk of unnoticed injury

key_questions.question: Any rash in your groin, on your hands, or elsewhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Tinea cruris or tinea manuum, which often accompany tinea pedis

reasoning_points: Itchy, scaly, peeling rash that begins in the toe web spaces, especially between the fourth and fifth toes
Maceration, fissuring, or a moccasin-like pattern of scaling on the sole
Exposure to damp communal floors such as locker rooms, showers, or pool decks
Risk factors such as hyperhidrosis, occlusive footwear, diabetes, or immunosuppression
Associated onychomycosis or tinea cruris supporting a dermatophyte process
No fever, spreading erythema, purulence, or severe pain to suggest bacterial cellulitis
KOH microscopy showing branching septate hyphae confirms the diagnosis

easy: Classic itchy, peeling rash between the fourth and fifth toes
Recent exposure to locker room or pool floors
medium: Moccasin distribution of dry scaling on the sole without prominent interdigital findings
Older adult with dry, cracked soles mistaken for dry skin
Partial improvement with over-the-counter antifungal cream
hard: Patient with diabetes and neuropathy where itching is blunted and the rash is extensive
Immunocompromised patient with widespread sole and dorsum involvement
Vesicular or bullous presentation on the instep mimicking dyshidrotic eczema
Rash that fails topical therapy and requires KOH or culture to separate from psoriasis or contact dermatitis
Secondary bacterial cellulitis complicating the picture
